subject: geography

questions.content: What does globalisation mean?
options: The growing connection and interdependence of countries through flows of goods, money, people and ideas
The decline of trade between countries
Governments controlling all industries
Everyone living in one country
questions.explanation: Globalisation is the process of increasing worldwide connections. It involves trade, investment, migration and information flows.

questions.content: What is a transnational corporation (TNC)?
options: A company that sells only within its own city
A government department
A charity that does not earn money
A company that operates in more than one country
questions.explanation: TNCs have offices, factories or shops in several countries and often have global supply chains.

questions.content: A tax added to imported goods is called a
options: Quota
Subsidy
Tariff
Dividend
questions.explanation: A tariff makes imports more expensive so home-produced goods become relatively cheaper. A quota limits quantities.

questions.content: Which of these is an example of a regional trading bloc?
options: The Sahara
The European Union
The United Nations Children's Fund
A shipping container
questions.explanation: Trading blocs are groups of countries that reduce trade barriers among themselves. The EU is the best known.

questions.content: Foreign direct investment (FDI) occurs when
options: A company from one country sets up or buys business operations in another country
A tourist buys souvenirs abroad
A government cancels a debt
A worker sends money home
questions.explanation: FDI involves building factories, shops or offices abroad or buying a share in foreign firms.

questions.content: A smartphone is designed in one country, its parts are made in several others and it is assembled in another. This is an example of
options: A local monopoly
Import substitution
A trade embargo
A global supply chain
questions.explanation: Different stages of production take place in different countries to use skills, costs or resources where they are best.

questions.content: Why do many TNCs locate factories in lower-income countries?
options: Wages are always higher there
To avoid using any raw materials
Labour costs are often lower and there may be incentives such as tax breaks
Because shipping is impossible from high-income countries
questions.explanation: Lower costs increase profit. However, workers may face poor conditions, so the benefit is debated.

questions.content: Which of these is a likely BENEFIT of FDI for a host country?
options: Guaranteed higher wages for all workers
New jobs and skills, and increased exports
Complete control of the company by local government
No profits leaving the country
questions.explanation: FDI can create jobs and improve skills and technology. However, profits are often sent back to the home country.

questions.content: In 2021 the container ship Ever Given blocked the Suez Canal for about six days. What does this show about global supply chains?
options: A single disruption in a key route can delay trade worldwide
Supply chains never depend on shipping
Canals have no effect on trade
Ships are no longer used for trade
questions.explanation: The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean and Red Sea. The blockage held up hundreds of ships and showed the fragility of just-in-time supply.

questions.content: What is meant by comparative advantage?
options: A country is the best at producing everything
A country does not trade with others
A country produces goods only for itself
A country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
questions.explanation: Countries gain by specialising in goods where their opportunity cost is lower and trading for the rest.

questions.content: A country exported goods worth $320 billion and imported goods worth $350 billion. What is its balance of trade in goods?
options: A surplus of $30 billion
A surplus of $670 billion
A deficit of $30 billion
A deficit of $350 billion
questions.explanation: Exports minus imports = 320 − 350 = −30, so a trade deficit of $30 billion.

questions.content: Which is the best argument AGAINST rapid globalisation?
options: It makes all goods more expensive for everyone
Local industries may be unable to compete and workers can lose jobs or face poor conditions
It stops information being shared
It increases isolation
questions.explanation: Opening markets can hurt local firms and workers. Evidence on its effects is mixed so a balanced answer is needed.

questions.content: Fairtrade schemes aim to
options: Give farmers in developing countries a guaranteed minimum price and better working conditions
Raise the price of all goods to consumers by a fixed amount
Stop farmers exporting goods
End all use of cocoa and coffee
questions.explanation: Fairtrade standards include minimum prices and a premium for community projects. Critics note that not all benefit reaches farmers.

questions.content: A country imposes a 20% tariff on imported steel. Which effect is most likely?
options: Steel prices fall for all buyers
Foreign steel producers gain sales
The country will export more steel
Home steel producers gain a price advantage, but steel-using industries may face higher costs and may retaliate
questions.explanation: Tariffs protect home producers but raise costs for buyers, and trading partners may respond with their own tariffs.

questions.content: A clothing brand sources T-shirts from a factory in a lower-income country where workers earn the legal minimum wage, but pay is below a living wage. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The brand cannot be criticised if it follows the law
Minimum wage always equals a living wage
The factory complies with the law, but the brand could still be criticised ethically for low pay
Workers are not affected by supply chain decisions
questions.explanation: Legal compliance and ethical responsibility differ. Consumers and campaigners often press brands to pay a living wage.

questions.content: A TNC announces it will move production from Country A to Country B. In Country A, 2,000 jobs are lost. In Country B, 1,200 factory jobs are created, and local suppliers add 600 more. What is the total number of jobs created in B, and what is the net change for the two countries combined?
options: 1,200 created in B; net change −800
1,800 jobs created in B; net change −200
1,800 created in B; net change +200
2,000 created in B; net change 0
questions.explanation: Jobs in B = 1,200 + 600 = 1,800. Net = 1,800 − 2,000 = −200. Forgetting the supplier jobs gives −800.

questions.content: Evaluate: 'Trade barriers should be removed so every country benefits equally.' Which response is strongest?
options: Free trade can raise efficiency and choice, but benefits are uneven and some industries and workers lose, so support measures are needed
It is true because all countries gain the same
It is false because trade never benefits anyone
It is true because tariffs raise government income for all
questions.explanation: A strong answer recognises gains and losses and that outcomes depend on a country's economy and policies.

questions.content: Just-in-time production keeps very small stocks of parts. During a sudden port closure, what is the likely effect on a factory using this system?
options: Output will increase because costs are lower
Nothing changes since stocks are huge
Prices must fall immediately
Production may stop quickly because there is little stock to fall back on
questions.explanation: Lean stocks save money in normal times but make firms vulnerable when deliveries are delayed.

note:
Globalisation is the increasing connection of countries and people through trade, investment, technology and migration. It means that events in one place can quickly affect many others. In this sub-topic we focus on the flows of goods, services and money.

## Trade
Trade is the buying and selling of goods and services across borders. Countries trade because they have different resources, skills and costs. **Comparative advantage** means a country can make something at a lower opportunity cost than another, so both gain from specialising and trading. The **balance of trade** is exports minus imports: a positive value is a surplus, a negative value a deficit.

Governments sometimes use trade barriers:
- **Tariffs**: taxes on imports that raise their price
- **Quotas**: limits on the quantity of imports
- **Subsidies**: payments to home producers to lower their prices

Trade barriers protect local jobs but can raise prices and lead to retaliation. Countries often form **trading blocs** such as the European Union or ASEAN to lower barriers between members. The World Trade Organization (WTO), set up in 1995, provides rules and a place to settle disputes.

## Investment and TNCs
**Foreign direct investment (FDI)** is when a business sets up or buys operations in another country. Transnational corporations (TNCs) invest abroad to reach new customers, use cheaper labour or resources, or avoid trade barriers. Host countries can benefit through jobs, skills, technology and tax income, and the **multiplier effect**, where wages spent locally create further jobs. Drawbacks can include low wages, poor conditions, profits sent abroad, damage to local firms and environmental harm.

## Global supply chains
A supply chain links all the stages from raw materials to the customer. A smartphone, for example, may be designed in one country, use minerals from others, have parts made in several places and be assembled elsewhere. Containerisation, which put goods in standard-size steel boxes, made shipping cheaper and faster and helped this pattern grow.

Long supply chains are efficient but fragile. When the Ever Given ship blocked the Suez Canal for about six days in 2021, hundreds of vessels were delayed. Just-in-time systems, which hold little stock, are especially exposed to shocks such as port closures, pandemics or conflicts. Some firms now diversify suppliers or move production closer to customers.

## Fair and ethical trade
Fairtrade schemes pay farmers a minimum price plus a premium for community projects. Many consumers and companies also pressure suppliers to improve wages and safety. Complying with the law is not always the same as being ethical, since legal minimum wages can be below a living wage.

## Evaluating globalisation
Winners often include consumers, skilled workers and countries that attract investment. Losers can include workers in industries that shut, farmers who cannot compete with cheap imports and people in places that remain poorly connected. The overall effect depends on the country, the sector and government policy.

## How this is examined
You may be given trade figures, a short report about a TNC, or a map of a supply chain. Typical tasks are calculating a trade balance or job totals, explaining why a firm chooses a location, and evaluating whether a change is good for different groups.

Exam tip: Name the stakeholders (workers, firms, consumers, government) and give one benefit and one cost for at least two of them before you make a judgement.

flashcards.back: The growing connection and interdependence of the world through flows of goods, money, people, ideas and technology.
A country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than others, so specialising and trading benefits both sides.
Value of exports minus imports. Positive = surplus; negative = deficit.
Tariff: tax on imports. Quota: limit on import quantity. Subsidy: payment to home producers to lower their costs.
A group of countries that reduce trade barriers among themselves, e.g. the European Union or ASEAN.
Foreign direct investment: a company sets up or buys operations abroad.
New jobs and wages create extra spending in the local area, supporting further jobs and businesses.
The linked stages of making and delivering a product, often spread across several countries.
Little stock is held, so a disruption such as a blocked canal can quickly stop production.

subject: geography

questions.content: What is migration?
options: The movement of people from one place to another to live, usually for a long period
The movement of goods by ship
The daily flow of data over the internet
A short holiday abroad
questions.explanation: Migration involves a change of residence. It can be within a country (internal) or between countries (international).

questions.content: Which is a PULL factor that attracts migrants to a place?
options: War in the home region
Drought and crop failure
Lack of healthcare at home
Better job opportunities
questions.explanation: Pull factors are attractions of the destination. War, drought and poor services are push factors.

questions.content: Which is a PUSH factor?
options: High wages abroad
Good schools abroad
Conflict or persecution in the home country
A welcoming climate abroad
questions.explanation: Push factors are negative conditions that make people leave.

questions.content: Money sent home by migrants to their families is called
options: Tariffs
Remittances
Subsidies
Royalties
questions.explanation: Remittances are a major source of income for many countries, for example the Philippines and Nepal.

questions.content: Which of these is an example of an information flow?
options: Video calls and social media messages sent between countries
A cargo ship carrying cars
A farmer harvesting wheat
A migrant boarding a train
questions.explanation: Information flows are movements of data, ideas and communication, often via the internet and mobile phones.

questions.content: Under the 1951 Refugee Convention a refugee is generally a person who
options: Moves abroad only to earn more money
Moves from one city to another in the same country
Travels as a tourist
Is outside their country and has a well-founded fear of persecution so cannot or will not return
questions.explanation: Refugees leave because of persecution or conflict. Economic migrants mainly move to seek work or better living conditions.

questions.content: The UK and several other EU countries opened their labour markets to workers from Poland and other new members after 1 May 2004. What does this show?
options: Migration is only driven by climate
Migration cannot be controlled at all
Government rules and agreements can strongly influence migration flows
Countries never change migration policies
questions.explanation: EU enlargement in 2004 allowed freedom of movement for workers, increasing migration from new member states to some older ones.

questions.content: Brain drain happens when
options: Unskilled people arrive in large numbers
Skilled workers such as doctors leave a country, reducing its supply of skills
A country imports too many goods
Schools close
questions.explanation: Source countries lose people they have trained, but they may gain remittances and returning skills.

questions.content: Which is a likely benefit of immigration to a country with an ageing population?
options: More workers of working age pay taxes and fill job vacancies
Fewer people of working age
Less demand for services
A reduction in the cultural mix
questions.explanation: Younger migrants can help balance the dependency ratio, though integration and housing need planning.

questions.content: M-Pesa, a mobile phone money service launched in Kenya in 2007, shows how
options: Phones prevent trade
Banks are necessary for all transactions
Information flows reduce income
Mobile technology can let people send and receive money without a bank account
questions.explanation: M-Pesa allowed users to transfer money by text message, widening financial access and supporting remittances within countries.

questions.content: What is meant by the digital divide?
options: The gap between daytime and night
Different screen sizes
The gap between people with good access to digital technology and those with little or none
A fault in an internet cable
questions.explanation: Access varies by income, location, age and infrastructure, so information flows are unequal.

questions.content: Globalisation sometimes leads to 'glocalisation'. Which example fits best?
options: A shop selling identical goods everywhere
A fast-food chain that adds local flavours to its menu in different countries
A country banning foreign brands
A language dying out
questions.explanation: Glocalisation means adapting global products to local tastes, mixing global and local cultures.

questions.content: Some critics argue that global media can cause cultural homogenisation. What does this mean?
options: Cultures become more alike as global brands, languages and media dominate
Cultures become more different
Cultures stop interacting
Every country has its own language only
questions.explanation: Homogenisation is the loss of local differences. Others argue cultures adapt and blend instead (hybridisation).

questions.content: Net migration for a city is calculated as immigration minus emigration. Last year 52,000 people moved in and 38,500 moved out. What is the net migration?
questions.explanation: 52,000 − 38,500 = 13,500, a positive net gain. Adding the figures would give the total movement, not net migration.

questions.content: Country X has a net outflow of 80,000 skilled workers over five years but receives remittances equal to 9% of its national income. Which judgement is most balanced?
options: The outflow has only benefits
Remittances have no effect on development
Remittances support families and the economy, but losing skilled workers may harm healthcare and industry
Skilled worker loss always makes a country richer
questions.explanation: Strong answers consider both economic benefits and social or skill losses and note the difference between short and long term.

questions.content: A rural region receives faster internet. Which outcome is the LEAST likely direct effect?
options: Easier access to online education
An immediate fall in the cost of fertiliser to zero
New home-based businesses
Better access to market prices for farmers
questions.explanation: Faster internet can improve information and opportunities, but it does not directly make inputs free.

questions.content: A news report says: 'Thousands cross the border due to drought and food shortages.' A student concludes these people are refugees under the 1951 definition. What is the best critique?
options: Drought and hunger are push factors, but the legal refugee definition focuses on persecution, so the label may not strictly apply
Drought is the only cause of refugee status
Anyone who crosses a border is a refugee
Refugees can never be affected by drought
questions.explanation: Environmental migrants face real hardship but are not covered by the 1951 definition unless persecution is involved. Precision with terms matters.

questions.content: Evaluate whether social media increases cultural understanding between countries.
options: It always increases understanding
It never has any effect
It replaces all other forms of communication
It can share ideas quickly and connect people, but algorithms and misinformation can also deepen stereotypes, so the effect depends on use
questions.explanation: A strong evaluation considers benefits and limitations, and who has access.

note:
People, information and culture also flow around the world. Migration, communication technology and the spread of ideas make countries more interdependent. This sub-topic looks at why people move, what the consequences are, and how information and culture travel.

## Migration
**Migration** is a long-term change in where someone lives. **Internal migration** happens within a country, for example from villages to cities. **International migration** crosses borders. Reasons are often explained as push and pull factors.
- **Push factors** are negative conditions at home, such as conflict, persecution, poverty, lack of jobs, drought or poor services.
- **Pull factors** attract people to a destination, such as jobs, higher wages, safety, education and family links.
Migration may be voluntary (choosing to move for work or study) or forced (fleeing conflict). A **refugee**, under the 1951 Refugee Convention, is someone outside their country with a well-founded fear of persecution. An economic migrant moves mainly to find work. Be careful to use these terms accurately.

Governments influence migration through visas, border controls and agreements. For example, after the 2004 enlargement of the European Union, workers from new member states such as Poland gained the right to look for work in several older member states.

## Impacts of migration
For the **source country** the benefits include remittances (money sent home), which can be a major source of income, and skills gained abroad. Costs include **brain drain**, when skilled people such as doctors leave. For the **destination country** the benefits include filling labour shortages, paying taxes and cultural diversity. The challenges include pressure on housing and services, and the need to support integration. Impacts differ by place, so avoid saying that migration is simply good or bad.

## Information flows
The internet, mobile phones and satellites let information travel almost instantly. Examples include video calls, online learning and financial services. M-Pesa, which started in Kenya in 2007, allows people to send money by mobile phone, even without a bank account. But there is a **digital divide**: poorer, rural or older people often have less access, which can widen inequality. Misinformation can also spread rapidly, so critical thinking about sources matters.

## Cultural flows
**Cultural diffusion** is the spread of music, food, language, fashion and ideas across the world. Migration, tourism, trade and media all drive it. Two views are common:
- **Homogenisation**: cultures become more alike as global brands and English-language media dominate
- **Hybridisation or glocalisation**: global ideas are adapted to local tastes, such as a fast-food chain adding local menu items
Many places experience both. Local traditions may weaken, but they can also be revived and shared worldwide through the same technologies.

## Calculations and data
Net migration = immigration minus emigration. Always check which number is bigger and give the sign. Population change also includes natural change (births minus deaths).

## How this is examined
Typical tasks show migration statistics, a news extract or a graph of internet use. You are asked to explain push and pull factors, calculate net migration, compare impacts on source and destination countries, and evaluate how information and culture flows affect different groups.

Common mistakes: using "refugee" and "migrant" as if they were the same; listing only positive or only negative impacts; describing homogenisation as if it were the only possible outcome.

Exam tip: When asked to evaluate, show both sides, name the groups affected (for example young people, employers, local residents) and finish with a clear judgement supported by evidence from the source.

flashcards.back: Push: negative conditions at home (conflict, poverty, drought). Pull: attractions of the destination (jobs, safety, education).
A person outside their country with a well-founded fear of persecution (1951 Refugee Convention), unable or unwilling to return.
A person who moves mainly to find work or improve living standards, not because of persecution.
Money sent home by migrants, an important source of income for many countries.
Loss of skilled workers, such as doctors and engineers, from a country when they emigrate.
Immigration minus emigration. Positive = net gain; negative = net loss.
Gap between those with good access to digital technology and those with little or none.
Spread of cultural features such as food, music, language and fashion between places.
Homogenisation: cultures become more alike. Glocalisation: global products are adapted to local tastes.
